title-group.article-title: Green Modifiers for Sustainable Kuzu Starch-Based Films: Tailoring Functional Properties

abstract.p: Studies have shown that the use of readily available and easily prepared modifiers can control the specific properties of the starch material, targeting those that are most beneficial for specific applications. Starch is one of the materials poised to replace traditional polymers in food packaging and wound dressings. However, its functional properties, including barrier properties, antibacterial and mechanical properties, need to be improved. Films made of kuzu starch cross-linked with citric acid and plasticised with glycerol were modified with various modifiers: Kalanchoe pinnata extract, silver nanoparticles in this extract, an extract additionally stabilised with a biopreservative, and chitosan. The effect of these modifiers on the chemical structure and morphology of the starch films, as well as on their barrier properties, thermal, mechanical, and bacteriostatic properties, was determined. Only films containing silver nanoparticles produced clear inhibition zones against Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli. Chitosan-containing films exhibited weak antibacterial activity, while no measurable inhibition zones were observed for unmodified starch films or films containing only Kalanchoe pinnata extract. No viable yeasts or moulds were detected on the film surfaces during the 14-day storage period under the conditions of the study. The starch film with chitosan had the highest tensile strength, while film with the Kalanchoe pinnata extract had the highest elongation. The film made of starch with Kalanchoe pinnata extract had the highest water vapour transmission rate and the lowest contact angle, while the film made of starch with chitosan had the highest barrier properties.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Due to growing knowledge about the health risks resulting from environmental pollution with chemical compounds produced from petroleum, including synthetic polymers, it is extremely important to replace them with natural compounds [1]. Polysaccharides, proteins, lipids, and active compounds derived from plants are also finding increasing use in the development of useful products. Among this, starch—obtained from various plants—is of particular importance. This polysaccharide, due to its unique functional, antimicrobial, hemostatic, and tissue regenerative properties, is often used to prepare edible films and wound dressings [2,3]. Furthermore, the kuzu starch itself, obtained from the root of Pueraria montana, contains compounds (puerarin, daidzein, daidzein, and rutin isoflavonoids) that have several pharmacological functions, such as hepatoprotection, neuroprotection, cardiovascular protection, estrogenic activity, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory potential, treatment of alcoholism, antidiabetic activity, and immunomodulatory effects [4]. According to the literature, such starch films can be an excellent base for obtaining wound dressings and, at the same time, for creating edible coatings for food [5] and packaging in general [6].

The use of medicinal plants, such as Kalanchoe pinnata (known as Bryophyllum pinnatum or Bryophyllum calycinum), also plays a significant role in industries that rely on natural raw materials. It is a plant that is widespread in India, Madagascar, Vietnam, Hawaii, Australia, New Zealand, and tropical Africa, and now, as an ornamental plant, in many other countries. Kalanchoe pinnata leaves and sap have long been used in traditional medicine to dress wounds, including burns, as they exhibit strong anti-inflammatory, bactericidal, fungicidal, and virucidal properties, and also have excellent regenerative properties for all types of skin lesions. Analysis of the composition of Kalanchoe pinnata showed that this plant contains active substances, including glycosides, saponins, tannins, bufadienolides, triterpenes, flavonoids, terpenoids, lipids, cardenolides, steroids, and alkaloids [7]. Nguyen et al. [8] indicate that it contains 620 phytochemicals belonging to various classes. These compounds have cooling, antiseptic, astringent, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, antiasthmatic, antidiabetic, antiulcer, gastric ulcer healing, immunomodulatory, hepatoprotective, antioxidant, antidiabetic, and even anticancer effects [8,9]. The antibacterial activity of Kalanchoe pinnata leaves is attributed to the presence of the compounds diethyl phthalate, squalene, phytol, dibutyl phthalate, and delta-tocopherol [10]. Furthermore, the composition of these plants has been found to contain macroelements (N, P, K, and Mg) and microelements (Na, Cu, Fe, and Zn) [11]. Due to the known medical effects of Kalanchoe pinnata, Farida et al. [12] proposed the use of these leaves to treat diabetic foot wounds. Radwan-Pragłowska et al. [13], in their research, used the antioxidant and hepatoprotective properties of Kalanchoe pinnata extract to obtain a promising chitosan blood-clotting agent for wounds associated with significant blood loss.

Knowledge of the composition of extracts from medicinal plants such as Kalanchoe pinnata has led to the conclusion that the reducing properties of their constituents (especially flavonoids) can be used for purposes other than medicinal purposes. They were found to be suitable for obtaining nanoparticles in a much more environmentally friendly manner than chemical methods. For this purpose, extracts from plants such as Aloe vera [14], Leucaena leucocephala [15], Citrus hystrix [16], Zingiber officinale [17], and others are used, thus obtaining nanoparticles of silver [18], selenium [19], platinum [16], zinc oxide [20], or titanium oxide [21]. In an era of increasing resistance of pathogenic microorganisms to antibiotics, nanoparticles of metals or their oxides with bactericidal and virucidal properties may be an effective solution in the treatment of many infections. The effect of many nanoparticles in packaging is also known, inhibiting food spoilage. Among these materials, silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) are of particular importance [22]. With the principles of a circular economy in mind, green methods for obtaining nanoparticles are desirable. Guleriya et al. [7] point to two distinct phases during nanoparticle formation using plant extract: a nucleation period, during which metal ions use high activation energy to form small nuclei, and a growth phase, during which the small nuclei aggregate, supporting nanoparticle growth. Stabilisation of the newly formed nanoparticles using compounds from plant extract is also important at this stage.

To our knowledge, there are only few reports on the use of Kalanchoe pinnata leaf extracts to prepare nanoparticles. Jagdish and Nehra [23] obtained ZnO nanoparticles using this method for the treatment of urinary tract infections. Sankareswaran et al. [24] synthesised nanosilica using Kalanchoe pinnata leaf extract for agricultural applications. The use of this extract in the synthesis of ZnO nanoparticles resulted in a smaller size, the presence of biomolecules on their surface, and better monodispersity than traditional chemical synthesis [25]. Furthermore, the ZnO nanoparticles obtained by the green method showed better performance in the photocatalytic degradation of the methylene blue dye under the influence of sunlight. Nandini et al. [26] obtained copper and selenium nanoparticles and demonstrated that this green method allowed the production of nanoparticles that did not have a negative impact on soil microorganisms. There are also a few articles that present the results of obtaining AgNPs using Kalanchoe pinnata extract [27,28].

In this study, AgNPs obtained using Kalanchoe pinnata bioreducers were used to modify the properties of starch materials with potential applications such as wound dressings or food packaging. It was assumed that their addition, as well as the presence of compounds contained in Kalanchoe pinnata extracts, would allow the production of materials with prolonged resistance to microbial growth. The potential to improve resistance to microbial agents by modifying kuzu starch with chitosan was also investigated.

Therefore, in this study, we examined films made of kuzu starch modified with a Kalanchoe pinnata extract, a solution of AgNPs suspended in a Kalanchoe pinnata extract, and an additional biopreservative containing benzyl alcohol, salicylic acid, glycerin, and sorbic acid, as well as films containing chitosan. The chemical structure and surface area of the resulting films, their thermal and mechanical properties, contact angle, water vapour permeability, and inhibition of pathogenic microorganisms were examined. The aim of this work was to assess whether simple methods (in line with the principles of green chemistry) could influence the parameters of the resulting films. All modifiers (except for purchased chitosan, which, as previously verified, could also be prepared from food industry waste [29]) were obtained and incorporated into the starch matrix without the use of complex and energy-intensive processes. Therefore, it was investigated whether the properties of the resulting material could be controlled by appropriately selecting modifiers, depending on the needs of the application. Particular attention was paid to the microbiological stability of the resulting films during storage, including the possible occurrence of yeasts and moulds on their surfaces. Therefore, we selected kuzu starch, chitosan, Kalanchoe pinnata extract, and silver nanoparticles, all of which have been shown to have antimicrobial properties. The study also investigated whether the incorporation of a biopreservative influenced the microbiological stability of the films during storage.

sec.title: 2.1. Materials
sec.p: Starch films were prepared using commercial Kuzu starch (Pueraria montana var. thomsonii (roots) (Terrasana, Leimuiden, The Netherlands), glycerol, and citric acid (Chempur, Piekary Śląskie, Poland). The 0.1 M AgNO3 solution (Chempur, Piekary Śląskie, Poland) obtained from fixanal was diluted to 1 mM. Chitosan (Ch) (Mn 171,000, degree of deacetylation 97% (MRI Gdynia, Poland)) and Ecokonserwant (biopreservative contained benzyl alcohol (77–86%), salicylic acid (8–15%), glycerine (3–6%), and sorbic acid (1–4%), ECOSPA sc, Warsaw, Poland) were used as received.

sec.title: 2.2.1. Green Synthesis of Ag Nanoparticles (AgNPs) Based on Kalanchoe Pinnata (K) Extract
sec.p: Fresh washed and cut Kalanchoe pinnata leaves (25 g) were placed in 100 cm3 of distilled water and kept at 90 ° C for 2 h in an oil bath with constant stirring (the method developed based on a modified procedure [14]). After filtering, 180 cm3 of 1 mM AgNO3 solution was added to the extract (20 cm3) and heated, stirring, for 24 h at 37 °C (in the dark to minimise AgNO3 photocatalysis). The change in colour to brown indicates the reduction of Ag+ to Ag0 [18] (Figure 1). The complete reduction of Ag+ to Ag0 was confirmed by a test with 1 M of HCl solution, which did not precipitate AgCl. As shown in Figures S1–S3, following the literature, the presence of AgNPs was confirmed by XRD and SEM with EDS (details of the apparatus are given in the next paragraph). Four peaks at 2θ values of 38.2, 44.5, 64.8, and 77.5 degrees in the XRD diffraction pattern were identified as originating from metallic silver and corresponding to values (hkl): the planes (111), (200), (220), and (311) of silver, respectively (Figure S1) [30]. Peaks at 32.4, 46.5, 54.0, and 57.7 2θ indicate the formation of silver oxides [30,31]. The determined size of the nanoparticles was 20 to 70 nm (Figure S2), which is comparable to the sizes of AgNPs reported by other authors [28]. EDX confirmed the presence of silver by a peak at 2.98 keV, which is characteristic and clearly identifiable [32] (Figure S3). FTIR spectra of centrifuged, methanol-washed, and dried AgNPs indicate the presence of biomolecules from the Kalanchoe pinnata extract on their surface (Figure S4). Bands corresponding to the stretching vibration of –OH (around 3400 cm−1), C-H (2930 and 2899 cm−1), -C=O (1705 cm−1), and C-O-C (1034 cm−1) were detected [33]. A broad band in the 3000–3500 cm−1 range may indicate not only the presence of OH groups derived from alcohols, phenols, and water, but also the presence of an amide moiety. The presence of a protein layer on the AgNPs surface is also confirmed by the band characteristic for the C≡C (2329 cm−1), CO-NH- (1553 cm−1) stretching vibrations, and the previously mentioned bands of C=O and C-O-C bonds. The OH and CH3 bending vibrations may be responsible for the peak at approximately 1398 cm−1, while the sharp peak at 1083 cm−1 corresponds to the stretching vibrations of the O-C and C-N bonds [33].

sec.title: 2.2.2. Preparation of Starch Films
sec.p: Kuzu starch solutions were prepared according to the method described previously [34] by dispersing 5% w/w starch, 2% w/w glycerol as plasticiser, and 0.5% w/w citric acid (used as a potential esterifying and cross-linking agent) in distilled water (for St) or water with Kalanchoe pinnata extract (for St+K) and AgNPs in Kalanchoe pinnata extract (for St+AgNPs). In the case of St+AgNPs+P, biopreservative (P) was added to the solution. For St+Ch, chitosan (Ch) was partially dissolved in water with citric acid prior to addition to the starch solution. Table S1 provides the exact composition of the solutions. These solutions were then stirred at 85 °C for 45 min to induce gelatinization of starch. The St and St+Ch solutions were white, the St+K solution was cream, and the St+AgNPs and St+AgNPs+K were light brown (Figure 1). The prepared solutions were sonicated in the six pulsed cycles (15 s sonication/15 s break) before pouring onto Teflon plates, while the films were formed by evaporating the water at 35 °C for 24 h. The films were conditioned in a desiccator at 50% humidity for at least 2 weeks prior to testing.

Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra of starch samples were collected in the range of 4000–600 cm−1 (32 scans) using a Nicolet Nexus FTIR (Nicolet, Markham, ON, Canada) with a MKII Golden Gate accessory (Specac, Orpington, UK) ATR sampling accessory.

Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) and Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) were used for samples surface examination. The surface features of the samples were examined using a Quanta FEG 250 scanning electron microscope equipped (FEI, Eindhoven, The Netherlands) with an ET secondary electron detector and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscope (EDS)-EDAX Genesis APEX 2 (Mahwah, NJ, USA). Before imaging, samples were coated with a thin (10 nm) gold layer to prevent charging. Several areas of each sample were imaged to ensure a representative assessment of the surface. All measurements were made at a constant accelerating voltage of 10 kV. EDS measurements were performed on samples not covered with an additional gold layer, and the accelerating voltage in this case was 30 kV. The Atomic Force Microscopy Nanoscope VI Dimension Icon from Bruker (Santa Barbara, CA, USA) equipped with an integrated silicon TESP-V2 tip/cantilever was used in tapping mode. The resonance frequency was ~300 kHz. The tip radius was 7–10 nm, and the cantilever was 123 µm long. Different areas of starch film surfaces were scanned to ensure representative morphologies.

The XRD analysis aimed to identify the presence of the crystalline structures of silver nanoparticles within the examined materials. This was performed using X-ray diffraction with D2 PHASER XE-T equipment (Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA), employing a Cu-Kα radiation source. The measurements were conducted in the 2θ angle range of 10 to 80 degrees, with a step size of 0.02 degrees.

The thermal properties of the starch films were determined using Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA). DSC measurements were carried out using Mettler Toledo DSC3+ (Barcelona, Spain), with sealed aluminium pans with a sample weight of 6–7 mg. The DSC measurements of the starch samples were performed from 25 °C to 180 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 and under N2 atmosphere. The maximum of the endothermic peak was taken as the phase transition temperature (T), while the area under this peak was set as the phase transition enthalpy (ΔH). The thermal degradation of the investigated films was carried out by thermogravimetric analysis of Mettler Toledo TGA/DSC3+ (Barcelona, Spain). The TGA curves were performed in a temperature range from 25 to 800 °C under N2 and for comparison under air atmosphere at a 10 °C min−1 heating rate.

The hydrophilicity of the samples was estimated via surface Contact Angle (CA) and Water Vapour Transmission Rate (WVTR). The static water contact angles were measured at room temperature using a DataPhysics OCA 15EC goniometer (DataPhysics Instruments GmbH, Filderstadt, Germany). A 2 mL drop of distilled water was used for each measurement, and a picture of the droplet was taken immediately after placing it on the sample surface. In addition, the contact angle was determined for 1 and 3 min of drop age. The contact angle decline rate (ΔCA/t) was also determined, expressed as the change in the surface contact angle over the minute. At least five measurements were made for each type of starch film. The WVTR was evaluated using a RADWAG MAX 60/1/NH moisture analyser (RADWAG, Radom, Poland) equipped with a permeation probe. Each film sample was mounted between two sealing rings and placed above a permeation cell containing a pre-weighed portion of distilled water (~9 g). After the cell, the unit was weighed and placed inside the analyser chamber. The measurement chamber was kept at 45 °C for 2 h. The mass loss from the permeation cell was recorded with 0.1 mg precision and plotted against time. WVTR was calculated using Equation (1):WVTR = (W1 − W2)/(tA)(1) where:

list-item.p: WVTR—water vapour transmission rate (mg cm−2 h−1),
W1—the mass of water remaining in the permeation cell after the first hour (mg),
W2—the mass of water remaining after the second hour (mg),
t—duration of the measurement interval (1 h),

sec.p: The 1st hour of testing was used to stabilise the measurement chamber. The permeability values were considered reliable after 1 h of conditioning at 45 °C. Due to variations in the thickness of the starch films obtained, the raw WVTR values were normalized by multiplying them by the mean thickness (L) of the respective sample (WVTR* = WVTR L), thereby yielding a barrier parameter that is independent of the film geometry, expressed in units of mg mm cm−2 h−1.

The mechanical properties of the samples were assessed by determining the tensile strength and elongation at break. A MultiTest 1-xt tester (Mecmesin, Slinfold, UK) with a 70 mm gauge length and a crosshead speed of 10 mm/min was used. The samples were prepared as 100 × 10 mm strips and with a thickness of about 0.3 mm. At least five samples were tested for each film formulation.

The microbiological stability of the films was assessed by evaluating mould growth on their surfaces (qualitative method). The susceptibility of the films to mould growth was evaluated using a qualitative method aimed at detecting viable yeasts and moulds on the film surface. For each film variant (St, St+K, St+AgNPs, St+AgNPs+P and St+Ch), sterile fragments (5 × 5 cm) were prepared and immersed in sterile flasks containing 25 cm3 of diluent. After contact between the film surface and the liquid medium, 1 cm3 aliquots were taken and poured onto YGC agar (Yeast Extract Glucose Chloramphenicol Agar), intended for the detection of yeasts and moulds. Plates were incubated under conditions appropriate for fungal growth (25 °C during 120 h), and the results were recorded based on the presence or absence of visible fungal colonies. The purpose of this assay was to qualitatively assess whether viable yeasts or moulds could be recovered from film surfaces during storage rather than to quantify fungal contamination. Therefore, results were recorded as the presence or absence of fungal growth. The evaluation was conducted at defined storage time points: on the day of sample preparation (day 0), and after 4, 7, and 14 days of storage under controlled temperature and relative humidity conditions. The procedure followed the principle of transferring microorganisms from the surface of the material to a sterile medium, consistent with the approach described in ISO 18593: 2018 [35]. The authors defined the size of the film fragment and the volume of diluent to ensure complete immersion of the samples and reproducibility within the study. This assay was intended to evaluate the microbiological stability of the films during storage and was not designed to determine their antifungal activity.

Antibacterial activity was evaluated using the agar disc diffusion assay against the reference strains Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 25923 (Gram-positive) and Escherichia coli ATCC 25922 (Gram-negative). The assay was performed according to EUCAST guidelines with minor modifications related to the use of starch-based film discs. These reference strains were selected to evaluate the antibacterial performance of the films against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria that differ in the cell envelope structure. The assay is based on the diffusion of antimicrobial compounds from a solid disc into the surrounding medium, resulting in inhibition of bacterial growth in susceptible strains [36]. Mueller–Hinton agar was poured into sterile Petri dishes to obtain a uniform medium thickness of approximately 4 mm. Bacterial suspensions equivalent to the 0.5 McFarland standard were prepared from 24 h cultures using a 0.85% NaCl sterile solution, and the inoculum was evenly spread over the agar surface using sterile cotton swabs. The disc diffusion assay was performed following EUCAST guidelines, with minor modifications related to the use of starch-based film disc. Discs (10 mm in diameter) containing the tested additives were placed aseptically on the inoculated agar. A starch film disc without any active additive (St) was used as a negative control. Plates were incubated aerobically at 35 °C for 16–18 h [37]. After incubation, inhibition zones were measured using a digital caliper (Beta Poland Sp. z o.o., Skarbimierzyce, Poland). Antibacterial activity was expressed as the inhibition zone area (mm2). The inhibition zone was calculated by subtracting the area of the film disc (78.54 mm2) from the total area of the growth inhibition zone [34,38].

Statistical analyses were performed in two stages. For the data on film properties, a statistical analysis was performed to assess the effect of the additive type on the mechanical properties and wettability of the starch films. Results are presented as mean values with standard deviation (SD). Calculations for mechanical properties were based on three independent measurements (n = 3), while for the contact angle, it was based on five independent determinations (n = 5). The differences between the tested film variants with respect to mechanical properties were analysed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). If statistically significant differences were found, a Tukey post-hoc test was performed to compare means between individual groups. For contact angle measurements, a two-way analysis of variance with repeated measures (mixed ANOVA) was used, with film type as the factor between subjects and measurement time (0, 1, and 3 min) as the factor within subjects. If a significant interaction was detected, a Tukey post-hoc test was performed for the dynamics of the contact angle changes, expressed as the angle decrease between 0 and 3 min. The level of statistical significance was established at p < 0.05. Calculations were performed in Microsoft Excel using the Real Statistics add-in (XRealStats). Microbiological test data were performed using non-parametric methods due to the non-normal distribution of the data and the presence of zero values. Results are presented as median values with interquartile ranges (Q1–Q3). Differences in the inhibition zone areas between the additives tested were analysed separately for each bacterial species using the Kruskal–Wallis test. When statistically significant differences were detected, Dunn’s post-hoc test with Bonferroni correction was applied. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: 3. Results and Discussion
sec.p: Citric acid was maintained at the same concentration in all film formulations. Its use was based on previous studies, demonstrating its ability to esterify starch and, through the formation of citric acid-derived diester linkages, to promote intermolecular cross-linking under suitable processing conditions [39,40]. Thus, the present experimental design was intended to compare the effects of the selected modifiers within the same citric acid-containing starch matrix.

The starch films were homogeneous on the macroscale, as visualized in Figure 2. There was a similar degree of transparency and a slightly brown colour when using the extract of Kalanchoe pinnata extract, which was intensified when the extract contained AgNPs.

The average film thickness ranged from 0.229 to 0.395 mm. Typically, the introduction of plant extracts into a biopolymer matrix, due to the presence of a large number of low-molecular weight chemical compounds, increases the thickness of the sample [41]. This relationship was observed for St+K and St+AgNPs+P (Figure 2). However, in the case of St+AgNPs, the thickness of the obtained samples was lower than that of the starch film itself. Typically, an increase in film thickness is observed when AgNPs are added to a starch matrix. However, the results obtained indicated that strong interactions occur between AgNPs and starch chains, resulting in a tighter starch packing and, consequently, a thinner film, as also shown by Ceballos et al. [42]. The additional introduction of biopreservative compounds caused the loosening of the polymer matrix and the increase of the thickness of the St+AgNPs+P film. Interactions between the -OH groups of starch and the -OH and -NH groups of chitosan also cause tight packing of the chains of both biopolymers, reducing the film thickness (0.277 mm).
The chemical structure of the obtained starch films was determined by ATR-FTIR.

As shown in Figure 3, the FTIR spectra of all starch films are generally similar. As expected based on the literature [43], the FTIR spectra showed the presence of all characteristic bands of starch cross-linked with organic acid. Kuzu starch films have a broad characteristic -OH stretching vibration peak at 3100–3600 cm−1, with a maximum around 3290 cm−1. In the case of St+K, St+AgNPs, and St+Ch films, a discrete shift of this peak maximum to about 3275 cm−1 can be detected, suggesting an increase in the number of hydrogen—bond interactions after the introduction of modifiers [44]. Peaks at approximately 2922 cm−1 and about 2886 cm−1 indicated the presence of methyl and methylene H-C groups, while the band at 1330 cm−1 range is caused by H-C bending vibrations [45].

The band observed at 1719 cm−1 corroborated the existence of carbonyl groups of citric acid. This band is compatible with the possible formation of ester linkages between the citric acid and starch hydroxyl groups. However, because residual free citric acid was not removed or quantified prior to FTIR analysis, the contribution of unreacted carboxylic groups cannot be excluded. Therefore, the FTIR results support possible esterification but do not independently confirm the formation or extent of a covalently cross-linked starch network. The significant increase in the intensity of this band for St+AgNPs+P results from the introduction of other organic acids, i.e., salicylic and sorbic acid, into the starch network along with the preservative. Absorption at a wavenumber of approximately 1640 cm−1 originated from the bending vibration of O-H, which is bound to water molecules in starch through hydrogen bonds [46]. Knowing that the band at 1415 cm−1 corresponds to deformational vibrations of C-O-H bonds in glycerine [47], its shift to 1408 cm−1 visible in the spectra suggests that glycerine effectively interacted with the starch matrix, creating a stable physicochemical system.

The lack of new peaks and only slight changes in their intensity and wavenumber shifts (marked in Figure 3) indicate that the organic compounds present in the plant extract influenced the physical, not chemical, structure of the starch. A similar conclusion was reached by Nguyen et al., who studied bacterial cellulose/PVA-based composite films incorporated with E. prostrata extract and silver nanoparticles, who also found no chemical reactions between the polymer matrix and plant extract compounds [48].

Most of the chemical groups that constitute the structure of chitosan and starch are similar in both compounds, hence their FTIR spectra are very similar [43]. However, in the case of St+Ch films, three characteristic bands at 1639 cm−1, 1583 cm−1, and 1336 cm−1 were attributed to the stretching of CO (amide I), and bending of N–H (amide II) and amide III groups in chitosan, respectively [49] (Figure 3). This suggests, at least partially, incorporation of chitosan molecules into the starch structure. Li et al. [50] showed in their studies that the use of a cross-linking agent allows the formation of chemical bonds between starch and chitosan molecules. The band at 1639 cm−1 overlapped with the band at 1640 cm−1 corresponding to bound water molecules, apparently increasing its intensity.

Looking at the ratio of peaks that indicate the crystalline structure of starch (1022 cm−1 vs. 998 cm−1) [51], it can be concluded that the highest crystalline fraction is found in pure starch and in St+AgNPs and slightly less in St+Ch and in St+K, and the lowest crystallinity is in St+AgNPs+P. It is hypothesised that the presence of chemical compounds in the extract of the Kalanchoe pinnata, particularly the extract of the Kalanchoe pinnata with AgNPs and a biopreservative, disrupted the ordering of the starch helix, resulting in a decrease in the crystalline fraction. Extracts of Kalanchoe pinnata contain many compounds with OH groups (e.g., polyphenols), which, by physically interacting with gelatinised starch molecules, hinder the ordering of its chains and recrystallisation. In the case of St+AgNPs, the OH groups of the plant components were consumed by the reduction of Ag+ ions, hence their lower presence in the extract and only a slight effect on the ratio of the 1022 cm−1 vs. 998 cm−1 peaks in the FTIR spectrum. In the case of St+AgNPs+P films, the addition of the biopreservative, along with its components, introduced new hydroxyl and carboxyl groups, which reduced the mobility of the starch chains and their recrystallisation. Similarly, the presence of large, three-dimensional chitosan molecules, through steric hindrance, impaired the ability of the starch chains to organise and form crystalline fractions.
The morphology of the starch films was examined by SEM and AFM and presented in Table 1 and Table 2, respectively.

The SEM micrograph of the St film showed that its surface is homogeneous and has a rough structure of fine pebbles with white inclusions of starch granules (Table 1). The same globular structure on the surface of the St film can be easily visualised in AFM phase images for 15 × 15 µm (Table 2). The use of plant extract during the formation of the St+K, St+AgNPs, and St+AgNPs+P films resulted in a significantly smoother surface, although it was interspersed with fine cracks. This was probably due to the formation of shorter starch chains as a result of reactions with low-molecular-weight components of the plant extract during film formation from a suspension of starch globules. The AgNPs incorporated into the St+AgNPs starch matrix interacted with the starch chains, introducing additional physical cross-linking, which improved the homogeneity of the resulting film and resulted in slightly fewer cracks. However, additional chemical compounds added to the starch suspension along with the biopreservative during film formation again reduced the film’s continuity, and the cracks on the St+AgNPs+P film surface were slightly larger (Table 1). As observed by AFM phase images (in both 15 × 15 µm and in high detail in 5 × 5 µm) of St+K, St+AgNPs, and St+AgNPs+P films (Table 2), the surface structure showed crystalline stacks (~500–700 nm) orientated parallel to the analysed surface. This type of surface crystalline structure is especially reached by adding K and P into the St matrix.

No cracks were observed on the surface of the St+Ch film. However, the addition of chitosan to the starch structure resulted in the formation of slightly larger and more regular pebble-like structures compared with the surface morphology of the St film, which is also observed by AFM. Meanwhile, Shapi’i and Othman [52] reported the opposite relationship: the introduction of chitosan into the starch matrix smoothed the film surface and the “pebbles” became finer. Presumably, the presence of the crosslinking citric acid hindered the mobility and ordering of the chains of both polymers during film formation, causing them to agglomerate. This affected the surface morphology.

The surface of the pure St film was lumpy and relatively rough (Ra 32.5 nm). This is typical of starch foils formed by pouring out a solution and evaporating water [53,54]. Concentrated amylopectin fractions are surrounded by a matrix containing mainly amylose. Interestingly, the introduction of the plant extract (St+K) resulted in a significant flattening of the lumps. This may be due to the formation of shorter starch chains as a result of the reaction with the plant extract compounds, which allowed them to arrange themselves in a more easily in the matrix without entanglement and agglomeration. However, the presence of AgNPs, which interact with the starch chains and the resulting network nodes, caused a further increase in the roughness. AFM images of the St+AgNPs and St+AgNPs+P films show distinct spherical AgNPs (marked with white arrows). The St+Ch film was characterised by the highest roughness, the reason for which was described during the analysis of SEM images.

It is known that branched amylopectin chains form double helices, which, when organised in parallel, create type A and type B crystallinity [55]. According to Gamarano et al. [56], type A and type B crystalline domains are formed from short terminal segments of amylopectin molecules with the same double-helix conformation, but with different packing arrangements and intracrystalline water content. The XRD pattern of the St starch film (Figure 4) shows one strongest diffraction peak at approximately 17° 2θ and smaller peaks at approximately 14.8° and 22° 2θ, which corresponds to type B crystallinity [55,57] and indicates that despite gelatinization and plasticization with glycerol, some starch crystallinity was retained. The visible reflection intensity at 2θ around 19.5°, associated with the amylose–lipid interaction [58], indicates recrystallization of amylose (VH type) as a result of the interaction with glycerol [56]. This is the so-called hydrated crystal structure. The introduction of plant extract and chitosan particles caused a significant reduction in the intensity of these peaks, and even their disappearance. This indicates that intermolecular interactions between the components limited the movements of the starch molecular chain segments and subsequently inhibited the crystallisation processes of the films [59]. The smallest changes in starch crystallinity were observed for St+AgNPs, while the largest crystallinity loss was observed for St+AgNPs+P. These observations are consistent with the analysis of FTIR results.
The thermal properties of the obtained films were determined using DSC and TGA.

Knowing that kuzu starch consists of 20–22% amylose and 78–80% branched amylopectin [60], it can be assumed that the crystallinity of obtained in these investigation films should be low. As shown by FTIR spectra and XRD analysis, the highest crystallinity was detected for the pure starch film and AgNP-modified film, and the lowest for the St+AgNPs+P film. Therefore, the high ΔH value of St and St+AgNPs films and the low value of St+AgNPs+P film seem to confirm these observations (Figure 5). However, as is well known, starch has a high tendency to bind water molecules in its structure. Therefore, the ΔH values correspond not only to the melting of the crystalline phase but also to water evaporation. This is confirmed by the results of thermogravimetric analysis and the derived thermogravimetric curves (Figure 6). Therefore, one broad DSC peak at approximately 100 °C should be considered as the result of overlapping processes: water vapor outflow and partial melting of crystallites, so the enthalpy under this peak is treated as apparent (total).

Thermogravimetric decomposition of starch films was carried out in air and inert gas (N2) atmospheres. The TGA thermograms are demonstrated in Figure 6A,B. Thermograms indicate that three main stages of thermal decomposition occurred in the N2 atmosphere as also known in the literature [61,62], while additional oxidation products of the film components were formed under the influence of the presence of O2 in air at temperatures above 400 °C. A general reduction in these temperatures was also observed when air atmosphere was used instead of N2. The first loss peak on the DTG curve (100 °C) is associated (as mentioned above) with the evaporation of crystalline water molecules contained in starch [63]. This stage mainly involved physical changes. The highest mass loss in this region was recorded for the unmodified starch film, indicating a higher water content compared to those of the other investigated films. Figure 6 and Table S2 also showed that the peaks corresponding to water evaporation significantly shifted toward higher temperatures after starch modification, indicating improved thermal stability. The films of modified starch reduced its affinity for water, with the greatest reduction for St+AgNPs and St+Ch films. This is in good agreement with previous results since FTIR spectra showed the increase in the intensity of the band corresponding to bound water (at 1640 cm−1) for the St+Ch film as an effect of overlap with the amide I bands (Figure 3), and not from the amount of water in the matrix. Bangar et al. [64] also noted that the introduction of nanoparticles (celluloic nanocrystals) into the starch matrix significantly reduced its tendency to bind water molecules.

Gradual mass losses were observed in the temperature range of 160–240 °C (for the study in air) and 190–270 °C (for the study in N2). This is a transitional stage in which the TG and DTG curves showed minimal fluctuations. Slow chemical reactions and recombination processes occurred within the starch film, preparing it for the next stage of intensive thermal decomposition [65]. The presence of O2 in the air slightly accelerates this process, hence the observed difference in the measured temperatures. On the other hand, Zhang et al. [65], based on in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (in-situ DRIFTS) analysis, found that during heating to 270 °C, no chemical reactions associated with breaking bonds or the formation of new ones between starch chains occurred, and mass losses of the samples in this range resulted from physical changes related to water loss. However, since more pronounced mass losses were observed for films modified with plant extract investigated, it was concluded that thermal decomposition of compounds extracted from plant extract also occurred at this stage [66]. In this temperature range (up to 270 °C), the mass of the St and St+Ch films decreased only slightly, which is probably related to the gradual loss of bound water and the degradation of glycerine and citric acid.

The largest changes indicative of thermal degradation were observed at 320 °C. When analysing the decomposition of wheat starch using in situ DRIFTS, Zhang et al. [65] found that it undergoes strong oxidation and decomposition reactions in this temperature range. Glycosidic bonds break down, glucose rings decompose, and gaseous decomposition products such as CO, CO2, and water vapour are released. Above this temperature, the previously formed carbon skeleton undergoes combustion and oxidation. In a nitrogen atmosphere, this mass stabilised at the end of the study, forming a carbon residue (from 8.4% to 15.6%), while in air, it burns almost completely. The maximum mass loss during the air test was observed at temperatures of 424 °C (St+AgNPs), 448 °C (St+K), 454 °C (St+AgNPs+P), 479 °C (St), and 537 °C (St+Ch) (Table S2). The introduction of chitosan particles significantly changed the complete burnout temperature of the carbon residue in the starch film. As shown by Barbosa et al. [67], the decomposition of chitosan with a similar degree of deacetylation was approximately 550 °C.

Table 3 shows that the temperatures at 5 and 10% weight loss increased significantly after the introduction of Kalanchoe pinnata extracts and chitosan particles, indicating an improved thermal stability of the modified films. This was observed for both N2 and air atmospheres. These changes are particularly pronounced for the modification of starch with chitosan. The temperature at 50% weight loss was comparable, approximately 310 °C. Only in the case of St+Ch film, the strong interactions between the starch and chitosan chains shifted it to 317 °C, confirming the higher thermal resistance of this film compared to others investigated films. The highest residue after thermal decomposition in an inert gas atmosphere was 15.6% for St+Ch film. The glucose and glucosamine ring structures that constitute chitosan undergo dehydration and condensation during pyrolytic combustion, forming a stable, carbon-rich solid structure. According to Zawadzki and Kaczmarek [68], thermal degradation of chitosan occurs primarily via a free radical mechanism, so radical intermediates can spontaneously recombine, resulting in the formation of cross-linked structures. Such cross-linked networks are more stable than linear chains and therefore may be present in the char residue, which accounts for its high content. Therefore, the presence of chitosan certainly had a significant impact on the increase in thermal stability. Such a large residue after thermal degradation cannot be due to the presence of chitosan particles alone, as they comprised only 6.25% of the total mass of the St+Ch film, while the difference in the amount of charred residue compared to pure starch was 7.1%. Therefore, the presence of chitosan must have caused an increase in the number of interactions (cross-linking) in the starch matrix (as indicated by FTIR spectral analysis), which, however, due to the steric hindrance of the chitosan molecules, did not lead to the formation of more crystalline forms. Liu et al. [69], while studying the Arenga pinnata starch—citric acid—chitosan system, found the formation of cross-linking between starch and chitosan, resulting in an increase in the mass residue and thermal stability of the obtained materials. In summary, the higher thermal stability and char residue of the St+Ch film most likely resulted from the combined effect of the intrinsic thermal behaviour and char-forming ability of chitosan and strengthened interactions between starch and chitosan chains. Hydrogen bonding and possible citric acid-mediated esterification may have promoted the formation of a more compact and thermally stable polymer network. However, the present analyses do not provide direct evidence of the extent of covalent cross-linking; therefore, these results are interpreted in terms of enhanced intermolecular interactions rather than confirmed chemical cross-linking.
The contact angle of the film surfaces was determined immediately after droplet deposition, as well as after 1 and 3 min.

The high contact angle of the St film results from the possible cross-linking of the starch chains with citric acid, as well as its highest crystallinity among the investigated films, as indicated by FTIR and XRD results. Starch hydroxyl groups, as a result of the reaction with citric acid, were acetylated, increasing the hydrophobicity of this polysaccharide [70]. Generally, the higher the hydrophobicity of the packaging material, the better the protection of packaged food [71]. However, the introduction of low-molecular-weight chemical compounds containing functional groups capable of reacting with starch and citric acid groups, along with the Kalanchoe pinnata extract, resulted in a reduction in the degree of cross-linking of the polymer matrix. Furthermore, the presence of these compounds with hydroxyl groups increased the affinity of the St+K film for water, resulting in a lower contact angle (Figure 7A, Tables S3 and S4). However, when OH groups (mainly from polyphenols) were used to reduce Ag+ ions to AgNPs (St+AgNPs and St+AgNPs+P), this effect was absent. The noticeable increase in the contact angle of these films, compared to St film, results from the involvement of starch OH groups, not bound to citric acid, in interactions with AgNPs. Furthermore, the introduction of chitosan chains, rich in hydroxyl groups, into the polymer matrix of the St + Ch film resulted in a decrease in the contact angle. To assess changes in the contact angle over time and compare the dynamics of these changes between the tested films, a two-factor analysis of variance with repeated measurements was performed. Material type was used as the factor between groups and measurement time (0, 1, and 3 min) was the factor between groups. Each value was the average of five independent measurements. The analysis revealed a very significant effect of time on the contact angle value (p < 0.001), confirming that all materials were gradually wetted. The type alone did not significantly affect the mean value of the contact angle (p = 0.108). However, a significant interaction was found between film type and the measurement time (p = 0.0001), indicating that the rate of change in the contact angle varied between the materials. Due to the significant interaction, a post-hoc analysis using Tukey’s test was performed, comparing the decrease in the contact angle between 0 and 3 min. Films containing silver nanoparticles (St+AgNPs) and silver nanoparticles with added preservative (St+AgNPs+P) were shown to have significantly higher wetting dynamics than films with added chitosan and plant extract (p < 0.05). This is confirmed by the highest values of the contact angle decline rate (Figure 7B). The results obtained indicate that the additives used did not significantly change the initial value of the contact angle but did affect the rate of water penetration into the material structure. This suggests that these films may be good material for dressings, where their increasing hydrophilicity will favour the absorption of water from wound exudates. However, when used as food packaging, they may quickly lose mechanical strength, unless the application is soluble packaging.

Determining the barrier properties of a polymer is important for estimating and predicting the durability of a packaged product when a starch film is used as packaging, as well as for proper wound healing when used as a wound dressing. Therefore, a low water vapour permeability value is a desirable feature [41]. The permeability of water vapor of a starch film is known to depend on several factors: the number of chemical groups with an affinity for water molecules (e.g., hydroxyl, carboxyl, amide groups), crystallinity, degree of cross-linking, molecular weight of the starch, the presence of plasticising agents, contact angle, and sample thickness [27], and, as indicated by Luduena et al. [72], structural defects on the sample surface. To compare the effect of additives on the barrier properties of the foil, the WVTR parameter was normalized by multiplying it by the thickness of individual samples, according to [73]. The relatively low WVTR* of the St film (4.30 mg mm cm−2 h−1) may be associated with citric acid-induced intermolecular interactions, possible esterification of starch hydroxyl groups, and the comparatively high structural ordering observed for this film. Because the degree of esterification or cross-linking was not quantified, the barrier behaviour cannot be attributed exclusively to covalent cross-linking. The introduction of low-molecular-weight compounds (including those with OH groups) resulted in an increase in WVTR* for films obtained with the Kalanchoe pinnata extract St + K (Figure 7B). However, when the plant extract also contained AgNPs, they hindered the diffusion of water molecules through the polymer mass, extending their path, which reduced the water vapour permeability (St+AgNPs and St+AgNPs+P). The tortuous path that water molecules must follow during evaporation, resulting from the presence of nanoparticles, is cited as the main factor in improving the barrier properties of films [74]. However, the additional presence of low molecular weight biopreservative components moved the starch chains apart, making it easier for the water molecules to penetrate, hence the increase to 5.29 mg mm cm−2 h−1 for St+AgNPs+P.

Meanwhile, the decrease in permeability of the St+Ch film is likely due to interactions between the functional group of St and Ch, as suggested by Zhong et al. [41] in their study of chitosan films modified with kuzu starch. These interactions resulted in strong physical cross-linking between the two polysaccharides, which hindered the diffusion of water molecules through the polymer mass of the film and reduced the WVTR. Li et al. obtained lower WVTR values for their starch—chitosan films cross-linked with glutaraldehyde (16.5 g m−2 h−1, which means 1.65 mg cm−2 h−1) [50]. Furthermore, starch—chitosan films cross-linked with citric acid and plasticised with glycerin but obtained under different process conditions, discussed in the article [61], were characterised by WVTR values up to 1925 g m−2 day−1, which translates to 8 mg cm−2 h−1.
The mechanical properties of the starch films were examined by determining the tensile strength and elongation (Table 4).

The tensile strength of the St film was 3.4 MPa, which is slightly less than that of the film obtained by gelation from the same substrates, but in different ratios and under different process conditions [59]. However, a higher elongation was obtained (58.5% vs. 32.6%). At the same time, the mechanical properties of the St film were slightly higher than those determined for the analogous corn starch, which were 2.8 MPa and 51.5%, respectively [75]. The replacement of part of the water during the formation of the starch paste with the extract of Kalanchoe pinnata (both alone and with AgNPs) resulted in a reduction in the tensile strength of the film. The low-molecular-weight components of the plant extract acted as plasticisers [41], slightly increasing the elasticity of the St+K film to 61.4%. However, strong interactions between starch chains and AgNPs in St+AgNPs films slightly improved tensile strength while simultaneously reducing elongation from 2.5 MPa to 3.0 MPa and from 61.4% to 56.9%, respectively, compared to the St+K film. The increase in tensile strength, accompanied by a decrease in elongation, when AgNPs were incorporated into a starch matrix, is known in the literature [62]. The St+AgNPs+P film, on the other hand, had the lowest tensile strength. Its tensile strength dropped to 1.2 MPa, which is consistent with the FTIR and XRD observations, suggesting the highest amorphous nature of this film. Although this film contained AgNPs, low-molecular-weight compounds containing hydroxyl and carboxyl groups were also incorporated. Instead of interacting with the OH groups in starch, the silver nanoparticles likely bound to the biopreservative compounds, thus negating the polymer network strengthening effect, and hence the significant reduction in the mechanical properties of this film. The deterioration in the mechanical properties of the films modified with the Kalanchoe pinnata extract was probably due to the cracks visible in the SEM images (Table 1), which disrupted the transfer of force during the sample stretching. However, a nearly two-fold increase in tensile strength, accompanied by a simultaneous decrease in elongation, was observed for St + Ch. The likely increase in interactions between starch and chitosan molecules, which form a specific cross-link, which caused the decrease in sample thickness and water vapour permeability, also affected the mechanical properties of this film. Similarly, Tan et al. [75] found that adding the same amount of chitosan particles to a corn starch film (also prepared with citric acid and glycerin) resulted in an improvement in tensile strength (from 2.8 MPa to 4.6 MPa) and a reduction in elongation at break (from 51.5% to 49%). Li et al. [50], examining their starch—chitosan films, also found that crosslinking between starch and chitosan limits the molecular motion of both macromolecules and may be the main reason for the reduction in elongation at break.

sec.title: Microbiological Resistance
sec.p: The control film (St), as well as all modified films, did not show visible fungal colonies at any of the time points analysed, including day 0 and after 4, 7, and 14 days of storage under controlled temperature and relative humidity conditions. The absence of detectable fungal growth throughout the storage period indicates good microbiological stability of the films under the applied experimental conditions, which is consistent with previous reports showing that starch-based materials can limit fungal development [76]. Lama et al. examined that, compared to wheat, rice, and corn starch, Kuzu root starch is characterised by higher resistance to fungal colonisation [77].

The antibacterial activity of starch-based films containing different additives was evaluated based on the inhibition zone area (mm2). Detailed median values, interquartile ranges, and minimum and maximum values are presented in Table 5, while representative images of bacterial growth around the film discs are shown in Figure 8.

In samples in which distinct inhibition zones were observed, antibacterial activity resulted from the diffusion of active compounds into the agar medium and was quantified as the inhibition zone area. No measurable inhibition zones were observed for the unmodified starch film (St) or the film containing Kalanchoe pinnata extract (St+K), while the chitosan-containing film (St+Ch) produced only small inhibition zones (Figure 8, Table 5).

Although kuzu root is a rich source of biologically active isoflavonoids, including puerarin and daidzein [77,78], previous studies have shown that the content of these compounds in kuzu starch depends strongly on the isolation and purification procedure. Commercially purified kuzu starch may contain only trace amounts of these phytochemicals, depending on the purification process [79]. However, although there was no zone of inhibition of bacterial growth around the St discs, microbiological resistance showed that the film did not become a medium for the development of microorganisms within 2 weeks. Therefore, no biological colonisation occurred. Therefore, it can be assumed in this preliminary approach that daidzein, this natural antimicrobial compound, is still contained in kuzu starch.

It can be assumed that St films may also act bacteriostatically, but without diffusion of active compounds from the starch material. Therefore, these results do not provide evidence that the native bioactive kuzu compounds made a measurable contribution to the antibacterial activity observed in the agar diffusion test. However, a minor contact-dependent or non-spreading effect cannot be completely excluded, but the pronounced antibacterial response should be primarily attributed to the incorporated silver nanoparticles in the case of St + AgNPs films.
The highest inhibition zones were observed for the films St + AgNPs and St + AgNPs + P, which exhibited a median inhibition zone area of 412.08 mm2 (Table 5).

The Kruskal–Wallis test revealed a significant effect of the additive type on the inhibition zone area of E. coli (H = 25.76; p < 0.001). Compared to the control film (St), only St+AgNPs and St+AgNPs+P produced significantly larger inhibition zones (Dunn’s post-hoc test, p < 0.05). In contrast, St+K and St+Ch did not differ significantly from the control and did not exhibit a measurable inhibition zone or only a small area (Table 5). Similarly, the Kruskal—Wallis test revealed a significant effect of the additive type on the inhibition zone area of S. aureus (H = 24.07; p < 0.001). The largest inhibition zones were obtained for St+AgNPs and St+AgNPs+P, with median values of 355.17 mm2 and 392.85 mm2, respectively (Table 5). Post-hoc analysis confirmed that both AgNP-containing films differed significantly from the control film (St) (p < 0.05). However, it was found that the addition of a biopreservative containing benzyl alcohol, salicylic acid, glycerin, and sorbic acid did not produce the expected significant improvement in antibacterial activity. The presence of AgNPs was primarily responsible for the observed antibacterial activity. These findings are consistent with previous reports showing that the incorporation of silver nanoparticles into starch-based films markedly enhances their antibacterial activity compared to unmodified starch films [74]. Similar antibacterial effects of AgNPs against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus have also been reported by Kim et al. [80]. The antimicrobial activity of silver nanoparticles has been attributed to multiple mechanisms, including disruption of the bacterial cell envelope, the release of Ag+ ions, and the induction of oxidative stress [81]. The larger inhibition zones observed for E. coli than for S. aureus may be related to differences in the cell envelope structure of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. The structural characteristics of the bacterial envelope, together with the interaction of silver nanoparticles with membrane components and the release of Ag+ ions, may contribute to the different susceptibility of these microorganisms to AgNPs [81,82].

To facilitate systematic comparison with previously developed starch-based materials, the mechanical properties, water vapour transport rate, wettability, and antibacterial properties of the films obtained in this study and selected formulations reported in the literature are summarised in Table 6. Because the reported values were obtained using different film thicknesses, conditioning protocols, relative humidity gradients, and antibacterial endpoints, they should be interpreted as method-dependent indicators of general trends rather than as directly interchangeable performance values.

The St+AgNPs and St+AgNPs+P films discussed in this paper produced significantly larger inhibition areas than those previously reported for kuzu films containing colloidal AgNPs, although differences in nanoparticle synthesis, concentration, dispersion, and release from the polymer matrix preclude attributing this difference to a single factor. Table 6 also provides, for comparison, the corresponding parameters of films prepared from other starch species. All of these data demonstrate that the botanical origin of starch is only one factor influencing the mechanical, barrier, and surface properties of films. Direct comparisons between different starch sources should be made with caution, as the reported values also depend on the amylose-to-amylopectin ratio, plasticiser and cross-linker concentrations, film thickness, conditioning conditions, and analytical methods used. Furthermore, it is clear that additives used to modify starch have an even greater impact on the properties of the resulting films, affecting both their antibacterial and physicochemical properties.

sec.title: 4. Summary and Conclusions
sec.p: Using ingredients with known antibacterial and health-promoting properties (kuzu starch, compounds contained in Kalanchoe pinnata extract, silver nanoparticles, a biopreservative, and chitosan), starch films were obtained that can be used, for example, as edible food coatings or wound dressings. The silver nanoparticles were obtained by exploiting the reducing and stabilising properties of the chemical compounds contained in the Kalanchoe pinnata extract. XRD and SEM confirmed the formation of nanoparticles with a size of 20 to 70 nm. The resulting starch films were characterised in terms of their chemical (FTIR) and structural (SEM, AFM, XRD), water affinity (CA, WVTR), thermal (DSC, TGA), and mechanical properties (tensile strength, elongation), as well as microbiological stability and antibacterial activity (zone of inhibition). On the basis of FTIR, XRD, and DSC studies, it was determined that the St and St+AgNPs films had the highest crystallinity, while the St+AgNPs+P film had the lowest, with the high water vapour transmission rate and the lowest contact angle immediately. Modification with Kalanchoe pinnata extract, AgNPs, and chitosan reduced the amount of water trapped between the starch chains, and this change was more significant after the introduction of chitosan molecules. Its addition also increased the thermal resistance of the starch film, its tensile strength, and its barrier properties. However, the presence of low-molecular-weight compounds from Kalanchoe pinnata extract and a biopreservative reduced the tensile strength, acting as plasticisers. Importantly, all films were found to be microbiologically stable, since no fungal growth was observed during storage. Antibacterial activity was observed for the St+AgNPs and St+AgNPs+P films, whereas only a small inhibition zone was detected for the St+Ch film. The difference in the inhibition zone size around the St+AgNPs and St+AgNPs+P discs was minimal, suggesting that the biopreservative did not provide a substantial improvement in antibacterial activity under the conditions of this study.

The research conducted showed that, depending on the desired specific properties of the films, simple and low-energy methods can be used to modify starch films to adapt them to the intended applications. Such technologies can be easily adapted to local conditions and are inexpensive, decentralised, and based on readily available raw materials. This is important for poorer countries, but also for those where there is a real threat of limited supplies of substrates, energy, or machinery, for example, due to geopolitical turmoil. At the same time, however, it is also a way to reduce environmental impact.

It should be noted, however, that before such films can be approved for production and use—whether in the packaging or medical sectors—specific, dedicated testing is required. This includes determining the precise concentration ranges of compounds extracted from Kalanchoe pinnata leaves, as well as the quantity of Ag nanoparticles generated. These factors are influenced by the plant’s growing conditions, such as sunlight exposure, soil quality, and irrigation. While these variables can be standardised in greenhouse cultivation, sourcing plants from the wild may result in a wide range of extracted compounds—and, consequently, a variable capacity to convert Ag+ ions into Ag nanoparticles. This necessitates thorough investigation. The same applies to the properties of kuzu starch, which also depend on variations in the composition of the Pueraria lobata root from which the starch is derived. Therefore, it is necessary to perform multiple repeated analyses of the composition of both the Kalanchoe pinnata extract (and, consequently, its Ag nanoparticle content) and the properties of the kuzu starch. It should also be investigated whether there are any conditions under which the composition of the plant material could lead to toxicity in the final product or prevent the intended properties from being achieved. Nevertheless, developing technology for the production of such starch materials, obtained according to the principles of green chemistry, may be one of the good solutions to replace synthetic polymers in various applications in the future.
